questions.q: What does the CMake function `pybind11_add_module` do that a plain `add_library` call does not?
options: It writes the C++ source code for you automatically
It sets the correct compiler flags and names the output so Python can import it as an extension module (e.g. the right suffix and ABI tag)
It removes the need to install Python entirely
It converts C++ templates into Python generics
questions.explain: `pybind11_add_module` wraps `add_library` with the extra configuration (compiler flags, output naming/suffix) needed to produce a module Python's import machinery recognizes.

questions.q: What is the role of `scikit-build-core` in a `pyproject.toml`-based pybind11 project?
options: It replaces CMake entirely with a pure-Python build process
It acts as the build backend that drives the project's CMake build when a user runs `pip install .`
It is a testing framework for C++ unit tests
It converts the compiled extension into pure Python bytecode
questions.explain: `scikit-build-core` is declared as the `build-backend` in `pyproject.toml` and invokes CMake under the hood so that `pip install .` compiles and installs the extension, rather than requiring the user to run CMake manually.

questions.q: Why can't a single compiled wheel work for every Python installation on every operating system?
options: Wheels are plain-text files and should work everywhere already
A compiled extension's binary embeds the target OS's ABI and the exact Python version's C API it was built against, which wheel tags (e.g. cp311-win_amd64) encode
pip refuses to install any compiled code as a matter of policy
NumPy blocks cross-platform wheel installation
questions.explain: A compiled extension is tied to the ABI and Python version it was built for; this is exactly what the wheel filename's tag communicates, and it's why cross-platform/cross-version distribution needs either a build matrix or source distribution.

questions.q: A teammate reports `ImportError: DLL load failed` when importing a pybind11 extension you built. What is the most likely class of cause?
options: The function names inside PYBIND11_MODULE were spelled in lowercase
A C++ ABI mismatch — commonly a Release/Debug build mismatch with the Python interpreter, or a missing runtime dependency
Python only supports extensions written in pure Python
The teammate's NumPy version is too new to use at all
questions.explain: DLL/shared-library load failures on a compiled extension are almost always ABI or runtime-dependency mismatches between how the extension was built and the environment it's being loaded into.

questions.q: What does `pip install -e .` do differently from `pip install .` for a pybind11 project?
options: It installs an encrypted version of the package
It performs an editable install, so local source changes are reflected without a full reinstall each time
It skips compiling the C++ source entirely
It installs the package only for the current Python session
questions.explain: An editable install (`pip install -e .`) links the installed package back to the local source tree, which is useful during active development so edits don't require a full `pip install .` each time.
